heuristics.rule: Target direct-hire Fortune 100 tech employers over IT consulting/outsourcing firms for H-1B sponsorship
heuristics.condition: When an international student is evaluating which employers to target for H-1B sponsorship
heuristics.action: Prioritize direct-hire tech and finance companies (avg 97.4% approval, 0.9% denial, 6.1% RFE rate) over IT consulting/outsourcing firms (avg 78.2% approval, 12.7% denial, 38.8% RFE rate)
heuristics.because: USCIS FY2025 data shows a 19.2 percentage point gap in approval rates and a 32.7 percentage point gap in RFE rates between these employer categories
heuristics.regulatory_basis: USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub FY2025; H1B Data Hub analysis of USCIS public disclosure data

heuristics.rule: Employer must register H-1B candidate by March 1–18 for October 1 start date
heuristics.condition: When an employer intends to sponsor a new H-1B worker subject to the annual cap
heuristics.action: Secure offer and complete employer registration during the March 1–18 USCIS registration window; offer and processing must be in place by February at the latest
heuristics.because: USCIS H-1B lottery registration window is fixed at March 1–18 each year; selected registrants then file full petition for October 1 start date
heuristics.regulatory_basis: USCIS H-1B Annual Cap and Lottery structure; USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub FY2025

heuristics.rule: Employer must pay whichever is higher: prevailing wage or actual wage
heuristics.condition: When an employer files an H-1B petition for any worker
heuristics.action: Employer must certify and pay either (1) the prevailing wage — average wage paid to similarly employed workers in the same occupation and geographic area — or (2) the actual wage paid to other workers with similar skills/qualifications, whichever is higher
heuristics.because: DOL prevailing wage requirement creates a legal floor; paying below this floor constitutes a violation of the Labor Condition Application (LCA) terms
heuristics.regulatory_basis: DOL OFLC Performance Data; DOL prevailing wage requirements for H-1B

heuristics.rule: Avoid IT staffing firms if H-1B approval certainty is a priority
heuristics.condition: When evaluating IT staffing firms as potential H-1B sponsors
heuristics.action: Treat IT staffing firm sponsorship as high-risk: approval rates of approximately 60–75%, denial rates approaching 20%, and RFE rates of 35%+
heuristics.because: USCIS FY2025 data identifies IT staffing firms as the lowest-performing employer category for H-1B approvals
heuristics.regulatory_basis: H1B Data Hub analysis of USCIS FY2025 public disclosure data

heuristics.rule: Verify employer H-1B history using USCIS Employer Data Hub before accepting offer
heuristics.condition: When an international student is evaluating a job offer from a potential H-1B sponsor
heuristics.action: Search the employer on USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub (uscis.gov/tools/reports-and-studies/h-1b-employer-data-hub) to see petition counts and approval history; also check DOL OFLC Disclosure Data for prevailing wages for the specific occupation and location
heuristics.because: Approval rates vary dramatically by employer; an uninformed acceptance of an offer from a low-approval-rate sponsor creates material immigration risk
heuristics.regulatory_basis: USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub; DOL OFLC Performance Data (dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/performance)

heuristics.rule: Cap-exempt employers are not subject to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap
heuristics.condition: When an international student is considering employment at a university, affiliated research institution, government research organization, or nonprofit research organization
heuristics.action: Recognize that these employers can file H-1B petitions at any time of year without lottery participation and without being subject to the 85,000 annual cap
heuristics.because: USCIS designates universities, affiliated research institutions, government research organizations, and nonprofit research organizations as cap-exempt
heuristics.regulatory_basis: USCIS H-1B Annual Cap and Lottery structure; USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub FY2025

heuristics.rule: Employer must be E-Verify enrolled to sponsor STEM OPT
heuristics.condition: When an employer is evaluating sponsoring a student on STEM OPT extension
heuristics.action: Confirm employer is enrolled in E-Verify as a separate requirement from H-1B sponsorship capability
heuristics.because: E-Verify enrollment is a distinct and mandatory requirement for STEM OPT sponsorship, separate from H-1B sponsorship eligibility
heuristics.regulatory_basis: USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub guidance; STEM OPT E-Verify requirement

decision_factors.factor: Employer type (direct-hire vs. IT consulting/outsourcing vs. staffing)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Employer category is the single strongest predictor of H-1B approval rate in FY2025 data, with a spread of over 37 percentage points between best and worst categories
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check employer against category benchmarks: direct-hire Fortune 100 tech (97.4% approval), IT consulting/outsourcing (78.2% approval), small companies <50 employees (65–80% approval), IT staffing firms (60–75% approval)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: USCIS identifies third-party placement as the single biggest red flag in H-1B adjudications, driving elevated RFE and denial rates across all IT staffing and body-shop consulting arrangements
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the H-1B worker will be working at the sponsoring employer's own location or placed at a third-party client site

decision_factors.factor: DOL Wage Level filed (I through IV)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Level I filings face RFE rates 5x higher than Level IV filings (34.2% vs. 6.8%); USCIS scrutinizes lower-wage positions as potentially not qualifying as specialty occupations
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify which DOL wage level the employer is certifying on the LCA: Level I (~17th percentile, entry-level), Level II (some experience), Level III (experienced), Level IV (~67th percentile, fully competent independent judgment)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: High-volume employers (e.g., Amazon: 4,644 approvals; Meta: 1,555; Microsoft: 1,394; Google: 1,050) demonstrate established H-1B infrastructure and consistent USCIS processing relationships
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub for number of new H-1B petitions approved in FY2025

decision_factors.why_it_matters: 20,000 of the 85,000 annual H-1B cap slots are reserved exclusively for US advanced degree holders, increasing selection probability relative to the general cap pool
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Confirm whether applicant holds a US Master's degree or higher to determine eligibility for the Master's cap exemption within the lottery

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A high RFE rate (e.g., Cognizant 38.8%, TCS ~37%) indicates a pattern of USCIS scrutiny that extends processing time, increases legal costs, and creates uncertainty even before a final denial decision
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check employer RFE rate via USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub or H1B Data Hub analysis; compare against category benchmarks (direct-hire tech: 6.1%, IT consulting: 38.8%)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Cap-exempt employers (universities, affiliated research institutions, government research organizations, nonprofit research organizations) are not subject to the 85,000 annual cap or lottery, eliminating the ~64.7% rejection rate from the lottery process
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the employer qualifies as a university, affiliated research institution, government research organization, or nonprofit research organization under USCIS definitions

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting H-1B sponsorship from an IT consulting or outsourcing firm
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: FY2025 data shows 12.7% denial rates and 38.8% RFE rates for IT consulting/outsourcing firms — even a successful petition may face USCIS challenges that delay start dates, increase legal costs, and create status uncertainty during adjudication
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who accept consulting firm offers as a fallback path to H-1B sponsorship, assuming any sponsorship offer is equivalent

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a Level I wage H-1B filing from an employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Level I filings face RFE rates of 34.2% — 5x higher than Level IV filings at 6.8% — meaning the employer's cost-saving wage decision directly increases the applicant's immigration risk exposure
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Entry-level international students whose employers file at the lowest prevailing wage tier to reduce payroll costs

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on the H-1B lottery for work authorization continuity
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: FY2025 data shows only a ~35.3% overall selection rate with 442,000 unique beneficiaries competing for 85,000 slots; approximately 300,000–350,000 qualified applicants are blocked annually purely due to cap limitations, not merit
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: All cap-subject H-1B applicants, particularly those without a backup plan if not selected in the lottery

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating salary upward from Level I to Level II or III
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: An employer who files at a higher wage level must legally pay that higher wage to comply with DOL prevailing wage requirements — the wage level on the LCA creates a binding legal floor, not just a benchmark
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who do not realize that their salary negotiation directly affects and is constrained by the DOL LCA wage level filed

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Working for a small company (fewer than 50 employees) as H-1B sponsor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Small companies have approval rates of only 65–80% and denial rates of approximately 15%, significantly below the 97.4% approval rate of Fortune 100 direct-hire tech employers
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who prioritize role fit, equity, or startup experience without accounting for materially higher H-1B approval risk at small employers

failure_patterns.pattern: H-1B petition filed by IT staffing firm placing worker at third-party client site
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: USCIS identifies third-party placement as the single biggest red flag in H-1B adjudications; body-shop and IT staffing arrangements face the highest scrutiny category
failure_patterns.consequence: Elevated denial rates (approaching 20%) and RFE rates (35%+); denial results in worker losing H-1B status and potentially falling out of authorized work status
warning_signs: Employer business model involves placing workers at client sites rather than internal projects
Employer is categorized as IT staffing or body-shop consulting

failure_patterns.pattern: H-1B petition filed at Level I (entry-level) wage
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: USCIS scrutinizes Level I filings as potentially not qualifying as specialty occupations; Level I RFE rate is 34.2% versus 6.8% for Level IV — a 5x difference
failure_patterns.consequence: RFE issued requiring additional evidence that the position qualifies as a specialty occupation; if RFE response is insufficient, petition is denied
warning_signs: Employer offers salary at or near the 17th percentile for the occupation and location
LCA wage level certified at Level I

failure_patterns.pattern: Candidate not selected in H-1B lottery despite qualified petition
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: FY2025: 442,000 unique beneficiaries entered for 85,000 available slots (5x oversubscription); selection rate approximately 35.3%; 300,000–350,000 qualified applicants blocked annually due to cap limitations
failure_patterns.consequence: Petition not selected; employer cannot file full H-1B petition; worker cannot obtain H-1B status for that fiscal year and must wait for next lottery cycle or find alternative status
warning_signs: Relying solely on H-1B lottery without backup status plan
Employer only participates in cap-subject lottery and is not cap-exempt

failure_patterns.pattern: Employer pays H-1B worker below certified LCA prevailing wage
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: DOL prevailing wage requirement mandates employer pay the higher of prevailing wage or actual wage; the LCA wage creates a binding legal floor
failure_patterns.consequence: DOL violation; potential back wages liability; employer debarment from future H-1B filings; adverse effect on worker's status
warning_signs: Employer salary offer falls below DOL OFLC prevailing wage for occupation and location
Employer requests worker accept reduced hours or unpaid periods

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the employer place H-1B workers at third-party client sites, or do workers perform duties at the employer's own locations?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the petition will face the highest USCIS scrutiny category (third-party placement) associated with IT staffing and body-shop arrangements
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Treat as high-risk H-1B sponsorship; denial rates approaching 20% and RFE rates 35%+ apply to this model
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Proceed to evaluate employer-specific approval and RFE rates via USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub

diagnostic_questions.question: What DOL wage level will the employer certify on the Labor Condition Application for this position?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the petition faces elevated RFE risk: Level I carries a 34.2% RFE rate versus 6.8% for Level IV
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If Level I: assess whether position genuinely qualifies as specialty occupation and whether negotiating to Level II or III is possible to reduce RFE risk
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Level III or IV: substantially lower RFE exposure; verify the salary offer meets or exceeds the certified wage level

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the employer cap-exempt (university, affiliated research institution, government research organization, or nonprofit research organization)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant must compete in the annual H-1B lottery (85,000 cap, ~35.3% selection rate) or can receive H-1B status outside the cap at any time of year
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: H-1B petition can be filed at any time without lottery; no cap exposure; proceed to evaluate petition-specific approval factors
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Applicant must be registered in March lottery window; only ~35.3% chance of selection; backup status plan required

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the employer's historical H-1B approval rate and RFE rate as shown in the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Employer-specific sponsorship reliability; whether the employer falls in the high-approval (direct-hire tech: 97.4%) or low-approval (IT consulting: 78.2%, IT staffing: 60–75%) category
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If approval rate above 95%: low immigration risk from employer-side; proceed to evaluate wage level and role specifics
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If approval rate below 85%: materially elevated risk; weigh against alternative offers from higher-approval employers

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the applicant hold a US Master's degree or higher?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Eligibility for the 20,000-slot Master's cap exemption within the annual H-1B lottery, which provides an additional selection opportunity beyond the general 65,000-slot cap
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Applicant is eligible for both the general cap pool and the Master's cap pool, increasing overall selection probability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Applicant competes only in the general cap pool of 65,000 slots; no additional lottery entries via Master's cap

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the employer enrolled in E-Verify?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the employer can legally sponsor STEM OPT extension, which is a separate requirement from H-1B sponsorship capability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Employer is eligible to sponsor STEM OPT; proceed to evaluate H-1B sponsorship history
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Employer cannot sponsor STEM OPT extension regardless of H-1B sponsorship willingness; student may lose up to 24 months of additional work authorization

industry_realities.common_belief: Any employer willing to sponsor H-1B provides equivalent immigration security
industry_realities.actual_reality: FY2025 USCIS data shows approval rates range from 97.4% (direct-hire Fortune 100 tech) to 60–75% (IT staffing firms) — a spread of over 37 percentage points; sponsorship willingness does not equal sponsorship success
industry_realities.implication: International students must verify employer-specific approval and denial rates via the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub before accepting an offer, not merely confirm willingness to sponsor

industry_realities.common_belief: H-1B denial is primarily about the individual applicant's qualifications
industry_realities.actual_reality: USCIS data identifies employer type and third-party placement model as the primary drivers of denial and RFE rates — IT consulting firms face 12.7% denial rates and 38.8% RFE rates regardless of individual applicant qualifications
industry_realities.implication: Choosing the right employer category is as important as individual qualification strength in determining H-1B petition outcomes

industry_realities.common_belief: A lower salary offer is simply a negotiation starting point with no other consequences
industry_realities.actual_reality: DOL prevailing wage requirements create a binding legal floor; an employer cannot legally pay an H-1B worker below the prevailing wage for their certified level; additionally, Level I wage filings carry a 34.2% RFE rate vs. 6.8% for Level IV
industry_realities.implication: Salary negotiation for H-1B workers is bounded by DOL wage levels on both the floor (legal minimum) and the risk dimension (wage level affects RFE exposure)

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B lottery is a meritocratic selection process where qualified candidates are approved
industry_realities.actual_reality: FY2025 data shows 442,000 unique beneficiaries competed for 85,000 slots (5x oversubscription); approximately 300,000–350,000 qualified applicants are blocked annually purely due to cap limitations, not qualifications or petition merit
industry_realities.implication: H-1B lottery non-selection is not a reflection of petition quality or candidate qualifications; backup status plans are essential given a ~64.7% non-selection rate

industry_realities.common_belief: Large Indian IT firms (Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro) are reliable H-1B sponsors because of their high petition volumes
industry_realities.actual_reality: FY2025 USCIS data shows these firms have among the worst approval rates: Cognizant 78.3%, Infosys 80.1%, TCS 79.6%, Wipro ~78% — with RFE rates of 36–39% — due to third-party placement models and lower wage level filings
industry_realities.implication: High petition volume does not correlate with high approval rates; candidates should evaluate employer-specific approval rates, not just petition counts

industry_realities.common_belief: FY2025 marks an improvement or stable environment for H-1B approvals
industry_realities.actual_reality: FY2025 data shows consistent year-over-year deterioration: overall denial rate rose from 4.9% (FY2024) to 5.8% (FY2025); RFE rate rose from 21.4% (FY2024) to 23% (FY2025); USCIS is identified as tightening scrutiny across the board
industry_realities.implication: The regulatory environment for H-1B petitions is becoming more restrictive year-over-year, increasing the importance of selecting high-approval-rate employers

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Asks 'Does this company sponsor H-1B?' and treats a yes answer as sufficient due diligence; assumes all sponsors are equivalent
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Looks up the specific employer on the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub to verify approval rate, denial rate, and RFE rate; compares against category benchmarks (direct-hire tech 97.4% vs. IT staffing 60–75%)
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Accepting an offer from a 60–75% approval rate IT staffing firm vs. a 97.4% approval rate direct-hire tech firm creates materially different immigration risk, even though both employers 'sponsor H-1B'

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Views consulting or staffing firm offers as valid H-1B pathways without recognizing that the work arrangement (not just the employer name) drives USCIS scrutiny
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Identifies that third-party placement at client sites is the single biggest red flag in USCIS adjudications; avoids IT staffing and body-shop arrangements specifically because the placement model triggers elevated denial and RFE rates
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: USCIS FY2025 data shows IT staffing firms face denial rates approaching 20% and RFE rates of 35%+ precisely because of the third-party placement model

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Negotiates salary purely on market rate and personal leverage, unaware that the DOL wage level on the LCA creates binding legal minimums and that wage level selection affects RFE exposure
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Understands that the employer must pay the higher of prevailing wage or actual wage; uses DOL OFLC data to verify prevailing wage for specific occupation and location; recognizes that Level I filing carries 34.2% RFE rate vs. 6.8% for Level IV and factors this into offer evaluation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The DOL wage floor cannot be negotiated below; additionally, accepting a Level I wage filing increases petition RFE risk by 5x regardless of individual qualifications

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: H-1B lottery timing and job search planning
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes an offer can be secured at any time during the year and H-1B processing will follow; does not connect job search timeline to the fixed March 1–18 USCIS registration window
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Works backward from the October 1 H-1B start date: knows the USCIS registration window is March 1–18; plans to have offer and employer processing ready by February; treats the lottery registration deadline as a hard constraint on job search completion timeline
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Missing the March 1–18 registration window means waiting a full additional year for H-1B status, potentially exhausting OPT work authorization in the interim

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats H-1B lottery selection as probable or likely given a strong application, or assumes that being selected is primarily a function of petition quality
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Knows FY2025 data shows ~35.3% overall selection rate with 442,000 beneficiaries competing for 85,000 slots; understands approximately 300,000–350,000 qualified applicants are blocked annually purely due to cap constraints, not merit; builds backup status plans accordingly
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Without a backup plan, the ~64.7% non-selection probability leaves an international worker without authorized work status despite a valid job offer and qualified petition

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Views universities and nonprofit research organizations as less desirable employers for career reasons without recognizing the immigration advantage of cap-exempt status
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Recognizes that cap-exempt employers (universities, affiliated research institutions, government research organizations, nonprofit research organizations) allow H-1B filing at any time without lottery exposure, eliminating the ~64.7% non-selection risk that applies to all cap-subject employers
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Cap-exempt employment eliminates the single largest source of H-1B uncertainty (lottery non-selection) and allows year-round petition filing
